messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Hari Patel

Hari Patel was forty-seven when his daughter Priya fell ill. She was nine years old, a bright-eyed girl who loved hiking the trails near their home in the Cascades where Hari worked as a park ranger. One October morning, after a family camping trip, Priya complained of a fever and severe headache. Within hours, her condition deteriorated. The emergency room doctors moved swiftly—spinal tap, antibiotics, the word meningitis spoken in urgent whispers. For three weeks, Hari sat in the pediatric ICU, surrounded by the sharp, chemical smell of antiseptic that seemed to permeate everything—the walls, his clothes, his own skin. He watched his daughter seize, watched her pupils dilate, watched machines beep in rhythms that no parent should have to learn. A resident with alcohol on his breath—Hari could smell it when the man leaned in to examine Priya one evening—had made a medication error that nearly cost her life. Only the quick intervention of a senior physician prevented catastrophe. Priya survived, but those three weeks had fractured something in Hari that no amount of gratitude for her recovery could repair.

In the months that followed, Hari found himself unable to move past what had happened. He replayed the moment he first noticed her fever obsessively, convinced that if he had recognized it sooner, she would never have been admitted. He dwelled on the resident's carelessness—the smell of alcohol on the man's breath became, in Hari's mind, a symbol of negligence, of how easily his daughter's life could have been stolen by someone's inattention. He spent hours in the evenings imagining confrontations, rehearsing what he would say to that resident, what he would do if he ever encountered him again. His wife, Meena, suggested they move forward, that Priya was healthy now, that Hari needed to let it go. But her words only deepened his conviction that she didn't understand the magnitude of what had been taken from them—what could have been taken. He began to dwell on her perceived lack of support during those hospital weeks, her occasional absences to work, her suggestion that they return to normal life. His rumination about her failings, about the resident's negligence, about his own delayed recognition of Priya's symptoms, became a kind of penance, a way of ensuring he would never be caught unprepared again.

This habit of relentless rumination, of turning every moment over in his mind searching for blame and missed warning signs, had begun to reshape his world in ways he didn't fully recognize. When he returned to work as a ranger, leading hikers through the forest trails he loved, he found himself hypervigilant in new ways. A tourist's dizziness on a steep trail sent him spiraling—his own head would swim, his vision would narrow, and suddenly he was back in the ICU watching his daughter's body betray her. The smell of a hiker's hand sanitizer would trigger the same chemical-sharp memory of the hospital. Even the lingering scent of someone's evening drink at a trailhead lodge could send him into a state of agitation that lasted hours. These sensations seemed to come from nowhere, but they were not random—they were the direct consequence of months spent dwelling on danger, on negligence, on the fragility of life. His mind, primed by endless rumination about what could go wrong, had become exquisitely sensitized to any cue that remotely echoed the trauma. A dizziness that a year ago would have been a minor inconvenience now felt like a harbinger. The hospital smell no longer meant cleaning; it meant the moment his world nearly ended. The alcohol smell meant the carelessness that almost took his daughter.

Hari had begun to avoid situations that might trigger these sensations—he volunteered for paperwork instead of leading hikes, he made excuses when colleagues mentioned getting a drink after work, he found reasons not to visit the hospital when Priya needed her follow-up appointments. When Meena suggested they visit her sister in the city, Hari's chest tightened at the thought of the hospital smell that would inevitably linger in those corridors. He had also come to dread conversations with friends or family who wanted to ask how Priya was doing, because their questions felt like reminders of his failure, of the resident's negligence, of all the ways he had not protected his daughter. His avoidance of these reminders—of people asking about the illness, of places that held the scent of his trauma—had begun to isolate him. His wife felt the distance growing between them. His colleagues noticed he had become withdrawn, unreliable on the job. The very strategies that had felt necessary to protect himself, to keep his mind vigilant against future disaster, had instead become the bars of a cage he was building around his own life.

Now, after nearly two years of this, Hari has finally agreed to seek help. He is afraid that if he stops dwelling on what happened, if he stops being vigilant, he will miss the next warning sign. But he is also afraid—though he speaks of this more quietly—that he is losing his family, that Priya, now recovering beautifully, is beginning to notice her father's fear whenever he looks at her.
